content.summary: Welcome to Unit 12. In this reading mission, you will explore personal narratives about first-time experiences, learn how to express regrets about the past using wish and if only, and master separable and inseparable phrasal verbs.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Using 'I wish / If only + past perfect' for past regrets, and future in the past structures.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Action-based phrasal verbs and descriptive vocabulary related to nerve-wracking experiences.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for specific emotional shifts in personal stories and understanding implicit cause and effect.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas and detailed events of B2-level narrative texts.
Recognize and interpret past regret structures accurately in context.
Identify and differentiate between separable and inseparable phrasal verbs.

contextWarmup.prompt: Think about a time you tried something completely new for the first time, like bungee jumping or public speaking. What is the most common reaction people have right before doing it?
options: Feeling nervous with physical symptoms like sweating and trembling
Staying completely calm without any emotional change
Forgetting that the event is actually happening
contextWarmup.explanation: First-time experiences of high stress typically trigger physical reactions like sweating, a dry mouth, and trembling due to adrenaline.

rules: I wish / If only + past perfect: Use this structure to express regret about something that happened or did not happen in the past. Example: 'I wish I had checked the weather before climbing.'

Separable phrasal verbs: The object can go between the verb and the particle, or after the particle. If the object is a pronoun, it must go in the middle. Example: 'blow the candles out' or 'blow them out'.
Inseparable phrasal verbs: The verb and particle can never be separated by an object. Example: 'I look forward to the trip' (correct) versus 'I look the trip forward to' (incorrect).

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often use the past simple instead of the past perfect after 'I wish' when talking about past regrets.
commonTrap.wrong: I wish I went to the party last night.
commonTrap.correct: I wish I had gone to the party last night.

paragraphs: Everyone remembers their first major adrenaline rush. For Mark, it happened on a sunny afternoon in New Zealand when he decided to try bungee jumping. Standing on the high platform above the turquoise river, he felt completely terrified. His hands were sweating, and his knees began to tremble as the instructor strapped the heavy rope around his ankles.

Looking back, Mark often thinks about that moment with mixed feelings. He managed to jump and survived the terrifying descent, but he regrets not buying the official video package. If only he had paid for the recording, he could show his grandchildren today. Instead, he must rely entirely on his fading memory to recount how he overcame his deepest fear.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Expressing Past Regrets and Managing Phrasal Verbs

content.summary: Practical guide on writing about past regrets using wish and if only, combined with proper placement of separable and inseparable phrasal verbs in descriptive paragraphs.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Expressing Past Regrets with Wish and If Only
blueprintItems.formula: I wish / If only + subject + past perfect (had + past participle)
blueprintItems.example: I wish I had studied harder for my final exams last semester.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Handling Separable Phrasal Verbs
blueprintItems.formula: Verb + Object (noun) + Particle OR Verb + Particle + Object (noun/pronoun)
blueprintItems.example: She turned down the job offer. She turned the job offer down.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Managing Inseparable Phrasal Verbs
blueprintItems.example: The manager is looking into the customer complaint.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always place object pronouns directly between the verb and particle in separable phrasal verbs.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I turned down it when the offer arrived.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I turned it down when the offer arrived.
mechanicsRules.why: Object pronouns like it, him, and them must sit between the verb and the particle.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not separate the verb and particle in inseparable phrasal verbs.
mechanicsRules.badExample: They looked the issue into before making a choice.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: They looked into the issue before making a choice.
mechanicsRules.why: Inseparable phrasal verbs require the particle to remain immediately after the verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use the past perfect tense after wish and if only when referring to unfulfilled past actions.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I wish I went to the conference last month.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I wish I had gone to the conference last month.
mechanicsRules.why: Regrets about past situations require the past perfect tense to show backward time shift.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: A First Time for Everything

content.summary: Mastering past regrets and future-in-the-past constructions requires precise control over weak forms, modal verbs, and sentence stress. When expressing regret with I wish and If only, speakers often use falling intonation to convey strong emotional weight and nostalgia. Furthermore, mastering separable and inseparable phrasal verbs ensures your delivery sounds natural and fluent during storytelling.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on linking auxiliary verbs to past participles in past hypothetical structures. Pay attention to how main verbs receive primary stress while auxiliary verbs and pronouns reduce into weak forms.

pillars.name: Intonation for Regret
pillars.target: Falling tone on final stressed syllables
pillars.explanation: Use falling intonation when uttering wish and if only clauses to signal sincerity and reflection on past actions.

pillars.name: Phrasal Verb Stress
pillars.target: Primary stress on the particle in separable verbs
pillars.explanation: In separable phrasal verbs like sort out, ensure the particle receives appropriate emphasis when standing at the end of a clause.

pillars.name: Connected Speech
pillars.explanation: When speaking quickly at B2 level, auxiliary verbs in past modal structures tend to blend smoothly into the preceding word.
